en: Abhidharmakośabhāṣyam, First Chapter: "The Treasury" (Kośasthāna).
Om! Homage to the Buddha.

Having paid homage to Him, the Teacher of reality, who has utterly destroyed all darkness in every respect and has lifted the world out of the mire of cyclic existence, I shall proclaim the treatise known as the Abhidharmakośa.
Abhidharma is pure wisdom together with its attendants; it is also that which leads to its attainment and the treatise [itself].
Because its meaning is fully incorporated into this [work], and because it is the basis for it, this is called the Abhidharmakośa.
Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions other than the discernment of phenomena,
and it is because of the afflictions that the world wanders in this ocean of existence, it is said that this treatise was therefore proclaimed by the Teacher for that purpose.
Dharmas are either with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava). Conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), excluding the Path, are with-outflows, because the outflows adhere to them.
The untainted [phenomena] consist of the truth of the path and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena:
space and the two types of cessation. Among these, space is that which does not obstruct.
Cessation through deliberation is disjunction, which occurs individually for each [defilement];
cessation not through deliberation is another, which is the absolute obstruction of arising.
Furthermore, those conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are the five aggregates (skandha), beginning with form (rūpa).
They alone are the time-periods (adhvan), the bases of discourse (kathāvastu), and they possess both an exit (saniḥsāra) and a causal basis (savastuka).
Those which are with outflows are the aggregates of clinging; they are also "with strife.
They are suffering, the origin, the world, the basis for views, and existence.
Form consists of the five sense faculties, the five objects, and unmanifest form;
the eye and so forth are the translucent forms that serve as the bases for their respective consciousnesses.
Form is twofold, or twentyfold; sound is eightfold; taste is sixfold;
odor is fourfold; and the tangible consists of eleven types.
That serial continuity, whether wholesome or unwholesome, which exists even in one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind,
and which is derived from the primary elements— that indeed is called non-informative action (avijñapti).
The primary elements are the earth element and the elements of water, fire, and air;
they are established by their functions of supporting and so forth, and are characterized by solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.
In worldly convention, "earth" refers to color and shape;
likewise, water, fire, and wind are also [merely] elements.
These same sense-faculties and their objects are held to be the ten bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
Feeling is experience; perception has the nature of grasping at signs.

The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), however, consists of those [factors] other than the [other] four; furthermore, these three, together with non-informative matter (avijñapti) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), are designated as the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Consciousness is the specific discernment [of objects], and it is the sense-base of mind;
it is also considered to be seven elements—the six consciousnesses plus the great element (the mind-base).
That consciousness which has just passed away immediately after the six [consciousnesses] is indeed the mind (manas).
For the sake of establishing a basis for the sixth [consciousness], the elements (dhātus) are taught as eighteen.
Everything is subsumed by one aggregate (skandha), one base (āyatana),
and one element (dhātu) through their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because they are devoid of extrinsic nature (parabhāva).

Because they share the same genus, object, and consciousness, the eyes and so forth constitute a single element (dhātu) despite being twofold; their emergence as a pair, however, is for the sake of beauty.
The aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) have the meanings of heap, entrance-door, and lineage, respectively.
The threefold teaching of the aggregates and so forth is due to the threefold nature of delusion, faculties, and inclinations.
Because they are the root of dispute and the cause of saṃsāra, and for the sake of establishing a sequential order,
feeling and perception are established as separate aggregates apart from the other mental factors.

The unconditioned is not mentioned among the aggregates because it does not fit their meaning; furthermore, the order [of the aggregates] is according to their coarseness, defilement, the analogy of a vessel and so forth, and their realms.
First, five [faculties] are listed because they have the present as their object; four because they have derived matter as their object;
the others because of their remote or more rapid functioning; or else, the order follows their respective positions.
For the sake of distinction, because it is predominant, and because it includes many primary dharmas,
one base is called "form" (rūpa-āyatana) and one is called "dharmas" (dharma-āyatana).
The eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma that the Sage proclaimed are either speech or names; they are included within the [aggregates of] form and mental formations.
Some say that the measure of a dharma-aggregate is the extent of the treatise; others say it is each individual discourse concerning the aggregates and so forth.
However, the dharma-aggregate is described as being the antidote to specific types of conduct.
In the same way, the other aggregates, bases, and elements should also be assigned as appropriate to those already mentioned, after having carefully considered their own specific characteristics.
The cavity is called the space element; it is said to consist of light and darkness.
The consciousness element is defiled consciousness; these are the bases for rebirth.
Among these, one is visible, namely form; ten are resistant;
eight are material and indeterminate, being those same [ten] excluding form and sound.
The others are of three kinds; all are included in the desire realm. In the form realm there are fourteen, excluding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.
The elements of mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness belong to the formless realm;
these three are both with outflows and without outflows, while the remaining ones are exclusively with outflows.
The five consciousness-elements are indeed accompanied by vitarka and vicāra;
the last three are of three kinds; the remaining ones are devoid of both.
They are non-conceptual with respect to the conceptualizations of discernment and recollection;
these two are respectively distracted wisdom of the mental faculty and all memory of the mental faculty.
The seven mind-elements and half of the dharma-element have objects;
nine are non-appropriated—those eight [elements] and sound; the other nine are of two kinds.
Tangible objects are of two kinds; the remaining nine material elements and a portion of the dharma-element are derived from the primary elements. These ten material elements are accumulated.
The four external elements both cut and are cut; they likewise burn and are weighed. Thus there is a dispute regarding the burner and the weighed.
The five internal [bases] are both born of maturation and accumulative;
sound is not born of maturation. Eight [bases] are non-obstructive; they are both outflowing and born of maturation.
The others are of three kinds; one possesses substance; the last three are momentary.
There may be the separate acquisition of the eye-element and the visual-consciousness-element, as well as their simultaneous acquisition.

Twelve are internal, excluding visible form and the others; that which is designated as "dharmas" is both sabhāga and tatsabhāga, while the remaining [elements] are those that do not perform their own function.
Ten [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation; five are [to be abandoned] by both [vision and cultivation]; the last three are of three kinds [vision, cultivation, and neither].
That which is non-afflicted is not to be abandoned by vision; nor is matter, nor that which is not born from the sixth [consciousness].
The eye and a portion of the dharma-element constitute the eightfold seeing;
the wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not seeing, because it does not judge.
The eye sees forms when it is "participating" (sabhāga), not that which is supported by it;
for consciousness, it is said, does not see forms that are obstructed.
One sees with both eyes because the vision is clearer;
the eye, ear, and mind have non-attained objects, while the other three [nose, tongue, and body] are otherwise.
It is held that the three [faculties] beginning with the nose grasp objects of equal dimension;
for the last one, the support is past, while for the five, it is simultaneous with them.
Because they undergo transformation according to the transformation of those [bases], the eye and so forth are the supports.
Therefore, because of their specific [unshared] nature, consciousness is designated by them.
The eye is not lower than the body; visible form is not higher than the eye;
and its consciousness [is not higher than either]. However, for the body, both [visible form and its consciousness] exist in all [stages].
Likewise, the ear belongs to three [realms], but all [the others] belong only to their own level;
body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower one, while the mind is indeterminate.

The five external [objects] are to be known by the [five] consciousnesses; the unconditioned phenomena are eternal; half of the phenomena (dharma-āyatana) are faculties, as are those which are remembered as the twelve internal [bases].
Thus ends the first treasury-location (kośasthāna), titled "Exposition of the Elements" (dhātunirdeśa), in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*:
"Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa."
"This was caused to be written by the venerable Lāmāvāka. This concludes the second treasury-location (kośasthāna).
Regarding the four matters, five [faculties] possess sovereignty; it is said that two [possess sovereignty] over two [matters].
Of the four, five, and eight [factors], in relation to defilement and purification.
The six faculties [are established] because they exercise sovereignty over the apprehension of their respective objects and over everything else;
furthermore, the female and male faculties are distinguished from the body faculty because they exercise sovereignty over femininity and masculinity.

The life-faculty, the five feelings, and the faculties beginning with faith are considered faculties by virtue of their sovereignty over the persistence of the group, defilement, and purification. (AKB 2.3)

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and likewise the faculty of "one who has known" [are established] because they exercise sovereignty over the successive attainment of higher stages and the attainment of nirvāṇa, respectively.
The basis of the mind, its differentiation, its duration, as well as its affliction,
its equipment, and its purification— to that extent there are faculties.

There are fourteen faculties [pertaining] to the process of existence (pravṛtti) by way of being its basis, its arising, its maintenance, and its enjoyment; likewise, there are others pertaining to cessation (nivṛtti).
The faculty of suffering is that bodily feeling which is unpleasant; pleasure is that which is pleasant.
However, in the third dhyāna, that same pleasant mental feeling is the faculty of pleasure.
Elsewhere, that [pleasant mental feeling] is mental satisfaction (*saumanasya*);

furthermore, the unpleasant [mental feeling] is mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*), while equanimity (*upekṣā*) is intermediate, being neither of the two because it is free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpanāt*).
In the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, there are nine, three, and three [faculties] respectively; these three are untainted (anāsrava).
The material faculties, the life-faculty, and the two painful faculties are tainted (sāsrava); the remaining nine are of both kinds.
Life-force is of two kinds as maturation; twelve [factors] are so, excluding the last eight and mental distress. That one [factor, mental distress] has maturation alone; ten are of both kinds.
The mind, the other sensations, faith, and so forth—these eight are wholesome; the mind and the other sensations are of two kinds;
the sensation of mental grief is of three kinds; and the others are of one kind.

Excluding the pure [factors], those pertaining to the desire realm; excluding the female and male faculties and the two [feelings of] suffering, those pertaining to the form realm; and excluding the two [feelings of] pleasure and all material factors, those pertaining to the formless realm.
The three mental feelings are of three kinds; the state of dejection is abandoned by two [paths];
nine are abandoned by cultivation; five are not to be abandoned; and the triad [of the mental organ and the two types of equanimity] is not [abandoned by cultivation].
In the desire realm, at the beginning, two results are obtained; not by those born spontaneously.
By them [the latter], six, seven, or eight are obtained; in the form realm, six; and one in the higher [formless] realm.
Upon cessation, in the formless realm one ceases vitality, mind, and equanimity;
in the form realm, eight; and in the desire realm, ten, nine, or eight.
In the case of gradual death, four [faculties] cease; in the case of a wholesome [death], five cease everywhere.
The attainment of the final two fruits occurs through nine [faculties]; for the other two, it occurs through seven, eight, or nine.

Arhatship is said to be attained through eleven [faculties], because it is possible for one person [to possess them all]. One who is endowed with equanimity, life, and mind is necessarily possessed of three.

One who possesses the body faculty possesses four [faculties]; one who possesses the eye or other [sensory faculties] possesses five; one who possesses the faculty of mental happiness possesses [those five] plus that one; one who possesses the faculty of physical pain possesses seven; and one who possesses the female faculty or others [such as the male faculty] likewise possesses seven.
One who possesses the faculty of having known (ājñātendriya) is endowed with eight or eleven;
one who possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is endowed with thirteen.
One who is devoid of all merit is endowed with at least eight [faculties]: the five sensations, the mind, the body, and vitality.
Likewise, an ordinary person in the formless realm is endowed with equanimity, vitality, the mind, and the wholesome [faculties].
One endowed with many [faculties] possesses nineteen, excluding the immaculate ones;
one who possesses both genders is a noble one (ārya) still subject to passion, possessing [nineteen] excluding two genders and two types of immaculate faculties.
In the desire realm, an atom that is soundless and devoid of sense-faculties consists of eight substances;
one possessing the body-faculty consists of nine substances; and one possessing any other faculty consists of ten substances.
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together with all the characteristics of conditioned phenomena;
or, mental factors are fivefold according to the divisions of the "great ground" and so forth, along with acquisition.
Feeling, volition, perception, desire, contact, discernment, mindfulness,
attention, resolve, and concentration are present in every state of consciousness.
Faith, heedfulness, pliancy, equanimity, moral shame, dread of blame,
the two roots, non-harming, and vigor are always present in the wholesome.
Delusion, negligence, indolence, lack of faith, lethargy, and restlessness are always present in the defiled; however, in the unwholesome, there are also shamelessness and lack of dread.
Anger, enmity, dissimulation, envy, spite, concealment, avarice, deceit, intoxication, and harmfulness are the mental states belonging to the limited level of affliction.
In a wholesome mind of the desire realm, there are twenty-two mental factors because it is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra; in some cases, remorse (kaukṛtya) is added as an additional factor.
In the case of unwholesome states that are unique (āveṇika) or associated with views (dṛṣṭi), there are twenty factors;
when associated with the four afflictions (kleśa), with anger (krodha) and so forth, or with remorse (kaukṛtya), there are twenty-one.
In the obscured [unwholesome] mind, eighteen [mental factors] are held to exist; in other neutral minds, twelve are considered present.
Since torpor is not incompatible with any of them, it is added wherever it may occur.
Regret, torpor, and the unwholesome states do not exist in the first dhyāna;
furthermore, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) do not exist in the intermediate dhyāna and those above it.
Lack of shame (*ahrī*) is disrespect toward what is blameworthy and a failure to see fear in it; lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is the same.
Affection (*prema*) is faith (*śraddhā*); respect (*gurutva*) is shame (*hrī*). Furthermore, these two [lack of shame and lack of dread] exist in the realms of desire and form.
Vitarka and vicāra are grossness and subtlety; pride is haughtiness; intoxication (mada) is the total absorption of the mind in one who is attached to his own qualities.
Citta, manas, and vijñāna have the same meaning; citta and the caittas have a basis, an object, and an aspect, and they are associated in five ways.
The formations dissociated from mind are: acquisition, non-acquisition, homogeneity, the state of non-ideation, the two attainments, vitality, and the characteristics.
The sets of names and so forth; acquisition (prāpti) is gain (lābha) and possession (samanvaya);
acquisition and non-acquisition pertain to those factors belonging to one's own continuum and to the two cessations.
The acquisition (prāpti) of dharmas belonging to the three time periods is of three kinds; for those that are wholesome and so forth, it is wholesome and so forth respectively.
For those dharmas pertaining to their own realm, it belongs to that same realm; for those not so pertaining, it is of four kinds.
The acquisition of those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naśaikṣāśaikṣa) and of those not to be abandoned is considered to be of three kinds;
the acquisition of neutral states is innate, with the exception of the superknowledges and the mind of emanation.

For obscured form in the desire realm, there is no prior possession; for non-defiled neutral [dharmas], there is no possession of the future. For past and unborn [dharmas], possession is of three kinds.

The non-acquisition of the paths belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as the untainted paths, is held to be "the state of being an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva). That [state] is abandoned through the acquisition of those [paths] and by changing one's level (bhūmi-saṃcāra).
Homogeneity is the similarity among sentient beings; the state of non-conception is [the cessation] among the non-conceptual beings;
and the cessation of mind and mental factors is a result of maturation; those [beings] are the Bṛhatphalas.
Likewise, the attainment of non-perception occurs in the final dhyāna through the desire for liberation;
it is wholesome, to be experienced only upon rebirth, not attained by an Ārya, and is acquired as belonging to a single time period.
Likewise, this [attainment] called cessation, born of the peak of existence, is for the sake of dwelling;
it is wholesome, associated with two feelings, and indefinite; it is attained by an Ārya through application.
The attainment of enlightenment by the Sage does not occur prior to the acquisition of the thirty-four moments;
it occurs when he has taken rebirth in the desire or form realms, and the so-called cessation [attainment] occurs first among humans.
Life is vitality; it is the support for both heat and consciousness.
Furthermore, the characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] are birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
The characteristics such as birth-of-birth (jātijāti) and so forth have these [eight] dharmas as their single object of activity.
Birth is that which produces what is to be produced, but not without causes and conditions.
The collections of names and so forth are aggregations of designations, sentences, and syllables;
they pertain to beings belonging to the desire and form realms, are out-flowings, and are likewise indeterminate.
Furthermore, that homogeneity (sabhāgatā) is also a result of maturation (vipāka); the acquisitions (āpti) are of two kinds;
the characteristics (lakṣaṇa), the outflows (niḥṣyanda), and the attainments (samāpatti) are non-acquisitions (asamanvaya).
The cause is held to be sixfold: the efficient cause, the co-existent cause, the homogeneous cause, the associated cause, the universal cause, and that called the retributive cause.

Factors other than themselves are the efficient cause (kāraṇahetu). Coexistent causes (sahabhūhetu) are those which are mutual fruits, like the primary elements, or like the mind and its concomitants, or like the characteristics and the characterized.
Mental factors, the two types of restraint, their characteristics,
and the mind itself are followers of the mind (cittānuvarttin) by virtue of time, fruit, wholesomeness, and so forth.
The homogeneous cause consists of similar factors belonging to one's own category and level that have arisen previously;
however, the Path of the nine levels acts as a mutual cause for those that are equal or superior.
Those born of application (prayogaja) are likewise [the causes] of those two; [factors] consisting of hearing, reflection, and so forth are also [their causes].
As for the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu), however, it consists of minds and mental factors that share a common basis.

Those called "pervasive" (sarvatraga) are the causes of all defiled states within their own level; the pervasive causes of the past are those [defilements] themselves. The ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) consists of the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows (sāsrava).
The pervasive cause and the homogeneous cause belong to two time periods; three causes belong to all three time periods.
Conditioned phenomena, along with dissociation, are the fruits; unconditioned phenomena do not have these as their fruits.
The fruit of maturation belongs to the last [cause]; the sovereign fruit belongs to the first.
The outflowing fruit belongs to the similar and the pervasive [causes]; the fruit of human effort belongs to two.
Retribution is an indeterminate dharma, pertaining to sentient beings, arising from what is determinate;
outflow is similar to its cause; and disjunction is the cessation [of defilements] through wisdom.
That which arises by the power of something else is the fruit born of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
That which is unconditioned (*apūrva*) is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of only that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Five [causes] grasp their fruit while present; two give [their fruit];
two are both present and past; one is past and gives [its fruit].

The afflicted, those born of maturation, the remaining, and the first noble [minds] arise respectively from all causes, excluding maturation and the omnipresent causes; those born of the remaining [causes] exclude both of those and the homogeneous cause.
Mind and mental factors, as well as others excluding the associated [factors], are taught to have four conditions; that which is called the "cause-condition" consists of five causes.
Minds and mental factors that have arisen, excluding the final ones, are the immediately preceding condition;
all dharmas are the object-condition; and that which is called the cause is known as the dominant condition.
When [a dharma] is ceasing, two causes perform their activity; when it is arising, three [causes do so]. The other two conditions, however, function in the reverse manner.
For the mind and mental factors arise from four conditions; the two meditative attainments from three;
and others from two. They do not arise from a creator god (īśvara) and so forth, nor from sequential causes and the like.
The primary elements are the cause of the derived elements in two ways; however, the derived elements are the cause of the derived elements in five ways.
The derived elements are mutually the cause of one another in three ways, while they are the cause of the primary elements in only one way.
In the realm of desire, the mind is wholesome, unwholesome, obscured, or unobscured;
in the realms of form and formlessness, it is other than unwholesome; and the untainted mind is of two kinds.
In the realm of desire, nine minds arise from a wholesome mind, and that [wholesome mind] arises from eight.
An unwholesome mind arises from ten, and from it, four [minds] arise; likewise for the obscured-unspecified mind.
From five [minds], the non-obscured arises; from that, seven minds arise immediately.
In the realm of form, eleven [minds] arise from the wholesome; from nine, that [wholesome mind] arises immediately.
From eight [minds], the obscured-unspecified arises; from that, six; from three, the non-obscured-unspecified arises again;
from that, six. In the formless realm, it is likewise; furthermore, from the wholesome, it is as follows.

From that [neutral mind], nine minds arise; from the obscured-unspecified, seven; likewise from that [unobscured-unspecified], seven; from four, the learner's mind arises; from this, however, five; but from the non-learner's mind, five arise.
Therefore, these four types of consciousness become twelve,
and by dividing the wholesome [consciousness] into two kinds— acquired through application and acquired at birth— within the three realms, they become twenty.

The neutral (avyākṛta) in the desire realm is fourfold: that born of maturation (vipākaja), that pertaining to postures (airyāpathika), that pertaining to the arts (śailpasthānika), and that pertaining to magical emanation (nairmāṇika). In the form realm, it is the same, excluding that pertaining to the arts.

In the defiled [minds] of the three realms, there is the acquisition of six, six, and two [faculties] respectively; in the wholesome [mind] of the form realm, of three; in the mind of one in training (śaikṣa), of four; and in its remaining [states], of the rest.
The second chapter of the Abhidharmakośa, titled "Instruction on the Faculties," is completed.
This is the third chapter of the venerable Lāmāvāka.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and the six classes of celestial dwellers constitute the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It consists of twenty divisions when distinguished by the various hells and continents.
Above [the desire realm], the form realm consists of seventeen distinct locations;
therein, each meditation (dhyāna) comprises three stages, while the fourth comprises eight stages.
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) has no physical location; it is fourfold by way of rebirth.
Therein, the continuum of mind (cittasantati) is dependent upon the group-homogeneity (nikāya-sabhāga) and the life-faculty (jīvita).
Among those [realms], the five destinies—hell and so forth—are designated by their own names;
they are exclusively non-defiled-neutral and are called "sentient beings," but the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not.
Those with diversity of body and diversity of perception; those with diversity of body and unity of perception;
their opposites, namely those with unity of body and unity of perception; and the three formless ones.

There are seven stations of consciousness; the remainder are characterized by their destruction. Together with the Peak of Existence and the non-percipient beings, these are known as the nine abodes of beings.
Furthermore, the four abodes are not other than the dwelling by choicelessness;
they consist solely of the four contaminated aggregates (skandhas) within their own respective levels.
Consciousness is not said to be a station; rather, it is included within the four alternatives.
Among these, there are the four modes of birth for sentient beings, beginning with those born from eggs.
Humans and animals are of four types; hell-beings, gods, and beings in the intermediate state are exclusively apparitional; and hungry ghosts are also born from a womb.

That which exists here between the state of death and the state of rebirth is the intermediate existence (antarābhava); because it has not yet reached the destination to be gone to, it is not [yet] "reborn" (upapanna).
Because of the similarity to the continuity of rice, there is the arising of existence without interruption;
however, the reflection is not a valid example because it is unestablished and because of its dissimilarity.

Because two [beings] do not exist together in one place, because there is no continuity [of the intermediate state], because it arises from a pair, because it is explicitly stated [in scripture], because of the mention of the *gandharva*, because five [factors] are mentioned, and according to the *Gati-sūtra*.
Because it is projected by a single [karma], this [intermediate state] has the form of the future existence of the previous time;
furthermore, it exists prior to death and subsequent to the moment of rebirth.
Visible to those of the same class and to those with pure divine eyes, possessing the speed of supernatural power through karma,
with all sense faculties intact, unimpeded, irreversible, and consuming odors— that is the intermediate state being (gandharva).
One with a perverted mind goes to the place of rebirth out of a desire for pleasure;
another, longing for odors and a dwelling place, goes with feet upward—such is the one bound for hell.
One enters with full awareness; another likewise remains [with awareness];
yet another departs [with awareness]; while another, who is always deluded, is born from an egg.

There are three types of descent into the womb for the Wheel-turning Kings and the two Self-arisen Ones (Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas), according to the sequence, due to the clarity of their karma, their knowledge, or both.
There is no self; there is only the aggregates, conditioned by afflictions and karma, which enters the womb through the continuity of the intermediate state, like a lamp.
The continuum, having increased gradually according to its projection, goes again to the next world through afflictions and karma; thus is the beginningless wheel of existence.
That dependent origination consists of twelve factors and three sections:
two each for the prior and subsequent limits, and eight in the middle for one who completes the full cycle.
The afflictions of the previous life are ignorance; the formative forces are those of previous karma;
consciousness is the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking; and name-and-form follows after that.

Contact exists prior to the arising of the six sense bases, and before that, prior to the coming together of the triad; it exists prior to the capacity to know the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Feeling (*vitti*) occurs prior to sexual union; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) belongs to one who is attached to enjoyment and sexual union;
grasping (*upādāna*), however, belongs to one who runs about in pursuit of obtaining objects of enjoyment.
That action which produces the fruit of future existence is "becoming" (bhava). Rebirth is "birth" (jāti), and from that point until sensation (vedanā) is "old age and death" (jarāmaraṇa).

This [twelvefold chain] is indeed intended as pertaining to the states of existence; however, the members are proclaimed according to their predominance, for the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the past, the future, and the middle.
The afflictions are three, karma is two, and likewise the seven are the basis;
this is a summary of cause and fruit, based on inference from the middle [two] of the two [extremes].

From affliction arise both further affliction and action; from that, the objective basis; and from that again, the objective basis and afflictions arise. This is the method of the members of existence (bhavāṅga).
In this context, "arising" (samutpāda) is considered the cause, and that which has arisen (samutpanna) is considered the fruit.
Ignorance (avidyā) is a distinct factor that is the opposite of knowledge (vidyā), just as the terms "non-friend" (amitra) or "untruth" (anṛta) imply their opposites.
If it is argued that [wrong view] is merely wrong wisdom because it is mentioned among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, it is not so;
for it is [separately] taught as a vision (*darśana*), because it is associated with vision, and because it is taught as a defilement of wisdom (*prajñopakleśa*).
The aggregates are indeed formless; there are six types of contact born from the coming together [of the three].
Five are contacts involving resistance; the sixth is called "designation-contact" (adhivacanasaṃsparśa).

The contacts of knowledge, ignorance, and that which is other than these are pure, afflicted, and the remainder; the contacts of ill-will and attachment, and the three beginning with that to be experienced as pleasant.
From those [six objects] arise six types of sensation: five are bodily and the other is mental.
Furthermore, that [sensation] is of eighteen kinds by way of the mental applications (manopavicāra).
In the realm of desire, all [consciousnesses] have their own [level] as their object; the form-realm consciousness has twelve as its range;
the higher [formless] realm is the object of three; and in the two dhyānas, twelve have the desire realm as their object.
The formless [realms] have their own [realm] as the object of eight; two [formless realms] are the objects of two; in the two dhyānas, however, there are six;
the desire realm is the object of six; four have their own [realm] as the object; and the higher [realm] is the object of one.
Four [mental applications] in the preparatory stage of the formless realm take form as their object; one goes upward;
one belongs to the fundamental stage and has its own sphere as its object; all eighteen are with outflows (sāsrava).
And what has been said, as well as what will be said later, is intended here to show that the afflictions (kleśa) are like a seed, like a nāga, like a root, like a tree, and likewise like a husk.
In those four states of existence, karma is like husked rice, likewise like medicinal herbs and flowers; the [resultant] entity is like prepared food and drink. (AK 3.37)

The existence at rebirth (upapattibhava) is defiled by all the afflictions belonging to its own level; the other three existences are of three kinds. In the formless realm, there are three [existences]. The world subsists on nutriment.
Edible food consists of three bases within the desire realm;
the base of visible form is not included therein, because it does not benefit its own sense organ nor those who are liberated.
Contact, volition, and consciousness—these three contaminated nutriments exist in the three realms.
The mind-made, the seeker of rebirth, the gandharva, and the intermediate state being [are synonyms for the being in the intermediate state].
In this context, two [types of karma] are for the nourishment of the basis and that which rests upon it;
the other two are, respectively, for the projection and the completion of another existence.

The cutting off [of roots of merit], their reconnection, the loss of detachment, death, and rebirth are held to occur only in the mental consciousness; moreover, death and rebirth occur within the state of equanimity.
These two [types of death] do not occur for one whose mind is one-pointed or who is without mind; they occur within the two neutral states.
In the case of gradual death, the departure of the mind occurs from the feet, the navel, or the heart.
The cutting of the vital points (marmaccheda) of those below, humans, and gods occurs through earth and the other elements;
these [beings] are fixed in rightness, fixed in falsity, noble ones, and those who commit the immediate transgressions (ānantarya).
In that regard, they maintain that the configuration of the receptacle world begins at the bottom with a wind-mandala, sixteen hundred thousand [yojanas] in depth and immeasurable in extent.
The depth of the waters is eleven thousand and twenty thousand [yojanas];
after that, the remaining height of eight hundred thousand [yojanas] becomes gold.
The circles of water and gold are twelve hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent, and three thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas] across.
Surrounding it, however, three times its size, are Mount Meru, Yugandhara,
Īṣādhāra, Khadiraka, and likewise Sudarśana.

Then there are Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka, and Mount Nimindhara; beyond these are the continents, and outside them is the Cakravāḍa range; seven of these mountains are made of gold, and that [outermost one] is made of iron.
Mount Meru consists of four jewels; it is submerged eighty thousand [yojanas] in the water, and rising above the water, Mount Meru is likewise eighty thousand [yojanas].
In the eight [continents], there is a reduction by half and half; they are equal in height and thickness.
There are seven intermediate seas between them; the first is eighty thousand [yojanas].
This is the inner ocean; it is three times as large on its sides.
The other Śītā rivers are each half the size of the preceding one, and the remainder constitutes the outer great ocean.
Therein, Jambūdvīpa measures three hundred and twenty-two thousand [yojanas];
it has three sides of two thousand [yojanas] each and is shaped like a cart.
Pūrvavideha is three and a half yojanas [in width] on one side; it is shaped like a half-moon.
Three of its sides are likewise [three and a half yojanas], while one side is three hundred and fifty yojanas.
Godānīya is seven thousand five hundred [yojanas] in circumference and circular;
the middle continent is two thousand five hundred; and Kuru is eight thousand, square and equal.
Deha, Videha, Kuru, Kaurava, Cāmara, Avara-cāmara, Aṣṭa, and Uttara-mantrin— these are the eight intermediate islands within it.
To the north of this, beyond the nine Kīṭa mountains, lies the Himavat;
fifty yojanas in width and length is the lake situated between [the Himavat] and Gandhamādana.
Below it, at a distance of twenty thousand [yojanas], is Avīci, which is equal in extent to that [world-system].
Above it are seven hells; thus all eight have sixteen secondary hells (utsada).
The Pit of Embers (Kukūla), the Corpse Pile (Kuṇapa), the Razor-Path (Kṣuramārga) and so forth, and the River (Nadī);
to the four directions of these are the eight others, beginning with Arbuda, which are cold.
The moon and sun are fifty-one yojanas [in diameter], being half the size of Meru;
midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise occur simultaneously.
In the second month of the rainy season, on the final ninth day, the night increases;
in the fourth month of the winter season, however, the day decreases, due to the reversal [of the pattern].
The increase of night and day occurs by moments as the sun moves southward and northward;
the moon appears diminished because of its proximity to the sun and its own shadow.
It has four terraces, each separated by ten thousand [yojanas],
which project outwards by sixteen, eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively.
On those [terraces] dwell the Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālādhāras, and the Sadāmadas;
and the Mahārājika gods also reside on the seven mountain ranges.
On the summit of Mount Meru dwell the Thirty-three; it extends eighty thousand [yojanas] in each direction.
At the intermediate corners are four peaks inhabited by the Vajrapāṇis.
In the center is the city named Sudarśana, made of gold, with sides of two thousand five hundred [yojanas] and a height of one and a half yojanas; its surface is variegated and soft.
There, the Vaijayanta palace has sides measuring two hundred and fifty [yojanas];
furthermore, it is adorned on the outside by the Caitraratha, Pāruṣya, Miśra, and Nandana groves.
Separated from these by twenty [yojanas] on each of the four sides are their excellent grounds;
Pārijāta is in the northeast, and Sudharmā is in the southwest.
Above that, in the celestial palaces (vimāna), there are six classes of gods who enjoy sensual pleasures;
they engage in sexual union through physical coupling, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.
Among these [heavenly realms], beings are born fully developed, clothed, and possessing form, appearing like infants from five to ten years of age.
There are three types of rebirths in desire: the gods of the desire realm together with humans.
There are three types of rebirths in happiness: the nine levels of the first three dhyānas.
From each level, as far down as it extends, so far up does it extend from that level;
they have no vision above, except by means of supernormal power or through the assistance of another.
A small chiliocosm is considered to consist of one thousand four-continent worlds, moons, suns, Mount Merus, abodes of the gods of the desire realm, and Brahma-worlds.
A thousand of those constitutes a second-order intermediate world system;
a thousand of those, in turn, is a third-order great trichiliocosm, which undergoes destruction and formation simultaneously.
The inhabitants of Jambudvīpa are four and a half cubits in height; those called Pūrva-videha, Godānīya, and Uttara-kuru increase by double each subsequent one.

The bodies of the gods of the Realm of Desire who possess form increase by one-quarter of a krośa at each level until they reach one and a half krośas; at the beginning, however, they are half a yojana, and beyond that, they increase further.
Above the Parīttābhas, however, the physical basis increases by half [of a yojana] at each stage;
from the Anabhrakas upwards, it doubles at each stage, with the exception of three yojanas.
The lifespan among the Kurus is one thousand years; in the two [other continents] it is reduced by half and half again respectively.
Here [in Jambudvīpa], it is indefinite; at the end it is ten years, and at the beginning it is immeasurable.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the lower gods of the desire realm;
by that reckoning, their lifespan is five hundred years.

For those above, both [the day-night cycle and the lifespan] double successively; furthermore, for the beings of the form realm, there is no day and night, but their lifespan is measured in aeons (kalpa) equal to the number of yojanas of their own bodies.
In the formless realm, the lifespans increase by twenty thousand eons each;
from the Parīttābha heaven upward, they are measured in great eons (mahākalpa), but below that, they are measured in half-eons.

In the six [hells] beginning with Saṃjīva, the days and nights are respectively equal to the lifespans of the gods of the desire realm; their lifespan is measured by those [days and nights] just like that of the gods of the desire realm.

In the Pratāpana hell it is half an intermediate kalpa, and in Avīci it is a full intermediate kalpa; for animals it is one kalpa, and for hungry ghosts (pretas) it is five hundred years, where a month [of theirs] is equal to a day [of ours].
The lifespan in the Arbuda hell is the time it takes for a cartload of sesame seeds to be exhausted by removing one seed every hundred years;
the lifespans in the subsequent hells increase twentyfold at each stage.
The Kurus, untimely death, atoms, syllables, moments, and the limits of matter, names, and time; likewise, the atom (paramāṇu) and the minute particle (aṇu).
Iron, water, rabbit, sheep, cow, hole-dust, louse-egg, and the barleycorn produced from that,
as well as the finger-joint, should be known to increase sevenfold each time.
Twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit; four cubits make one bow;
five hundred of these make one *krośa*, which is considered the distance for a forest hermitage.

They say that eight *yojanas* [make one *gavyūti*]; furthermore, one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* make one *tatkṣaṇa*. Sixty of those [tatkṣaṇas] make one *lava*; thereafter, each [subsequent unit] is thirty times greater than the preceding.
Three muhūrtas make an ahorātra; twelve months, together with the omitted nights (anarātra), make a year; and a kalpa is said to be of many kinds.
The eon of dissolution lasts from the cessation of hell-beings until the destruction of the receptacle world;
the eon of evolution lasts from the initial wind until the appearance of beings in hell.
An intermediate kalpa lasts from [the time when the lifespan is] immeasurable down to ten years;
thereafter, there are eighteen other kalpas consisting of periods of increase and decrease.
There is one period of increase until the lifespan reaches eighty thousand years;
thus, this world, having evolved, remains for twenty intermediate kalpas.
The periods of evolution, dissolution, and the state of having dissolved are equal;
these eighty constitute a great eon (mahākalpa), and [the lifespan of Brahmā] arises from three such incalculable eons.
For Buddhahood arises during the period of decline down to a lifespan of one hundred years;
Pratyekabuddhas arise during two such periods; and the Khaḍga [Pratyekabuddha] has been a practitioner for a hundred eons.
The appearance of a wheel-turning monarch does not occur when the lifespan is below eighty thousand years;
these wheel-turners possess wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron, respectively, in descending order.
They rule over one, two, three, or four continents; yet two do not appear simultaneously, as in the case of Buddhas.
They conquer by being welcomed, by their own journeying, by strife, or by weapons; they are non-violent.
The excellence of the Sage’s marks arises from their being well-placed, prominent, and complete;
formerly beings were like the gods of the Form Realm, but thereafter, gradually, through attachment to taste, they became as they are now.
Due to laziness, people made provisions for storage and hired field-guardians with insistence;
then, as the paths of unwholesome action increased, the lifespan decreased to ten years.
The end of the eon occurs through weapons, disease, and famine,
lasting for seven days, seven months, and seven years respectively.
Furthermore, there are three destructions by fire, water, and wind;
the second and subsequent dhyānas are their respective limits, in due order.
Because it shares the characteristic of being subject to swaying, there is no [unshakable state] in the fourth [dhyāna], due to its lack of immovability;
nor is it eternal, because its celestial palaces arise and perish along with the beings who inhabit them.
Seven [destructions] by fire and one by water; when seven such cycles by water have thus passed, there follow seven by fire, and after that, the destruction by wind.
The third treasury-location (kośasthāna), titled "Exposition of the World" (Lokanirdeśa), in the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya is completed.
Whatever merit is herein belongs to the venerable Lāmāvāka.
The fourth treasury-location begins.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
The variety of the world is born of karma; it consists of volition and what is produced by it.
Volition is mental action; that which arises from it is vocal and bodily action.
But those two, informative and non-informative [matter], are held to be bodily informative action;
it is shape, not motion, because conditioned things are momentary due to their instantaneous destruction.
Nothing could arise without a cause, and a cause would then be the destroyer [of itself];
it would be perceivable by two [senses], yet that is not the case for an atom. Vocal intimation, however, is simply the sound of speech.
By means of the statements regarding the three kinds [of form], pure form, increase, and the path of one who does not act,
it is established that after the first moment, non-informative form (avijñapti) belonging to the desire realm arises from past primary elements (bhūta).
Taking its own primary elements as its basis, bodily and vocal action is either with outflows or without outflows; where one is born, that non-informative [action] is non-appropriated.
That which is outflowing and designated as a sentient being arises from outflowing, appropriated primary elements;
that which is born of meditative concentration arises from developed, non-appropriated, and undifferentiated primary elements.
There is no indeterminate non-informative action; however, the unwholesome is of three kinds.
Furthermore, non-informative action exists in both the desire realm and the form realm, while informative action exists only in the two stages that possess discursive thought.

In the realm of desire, there is no obscured [unwholesome] state, because its origination is absent; liberation is ultimately wholesome, as are the roots [of goodness] and self-respect and dread of blame.
By association, those [factors] are so designated; by origination, actions and the like;
by the opposite, the unwholesome; and by the supreme, the neutral, which is eternal.
Origination is twofold, known as causal origination and simultaneous origination;
of these two, the first is the initiator and the second is the follower.

The consciousness to be abandoned by seeing is the initiator; furthermore, both [the mental consciousness and the fivefold sensory consciousness] to be abandoned by cultivation are followers. However, the fivefold [sensory consciousness] is only a follower.
For when the initiating [action] is wholesome and so forth, the conforming [action] may also be of three kinds;
however, for the Sage, it is always wholesome up to the point where neither [of the two] is born of maturation.
Non-informative action (avijñapti) is to be known as threefold: restraint, non-restraint, and that which is other than these.
Restraint is called Prātimokṣa, as well as that born of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and that which is untainted (anāsrava).
The Prātimokṣa is said to be eightfold, but in substance it is fourfold;
they are distinct due to the change of gender and name, yet they are not mutually exclusive.
Through the undertaking of abstinence from five, eight, ten, or all things to be avoided,
there arise the states of a lay follower (upāsaka), one who observes the fast (upavāsastha), a novice monk (śramaṇoddeśa), and a fully ordained monk (bhikṣu).
Virtue (śīla) is called good conduct (sucarita), action (karman), and restraint (saṃvara).
Furthermore, in its initial moment, it consists of both informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti) [matter], and it is the path of action (karmapatha) of the Prātimokṣa.
The eight [classes of persons] possess the Prātimokṣa; one who has attained meditative absorption possesses that which is born of dhyāna;
noble beings possess the untainted [discipline]; and the last two [types of discipline] follow the mind.
In the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya), those two called "abandonment" arise from the paths of immediate succession;
however, the two—clear comprehension and mindfulness—are the restraints of the mind-faculty.
One who abides in the Prātimokṣa is always endowed with the present non-informative [action] as long as it has not been abandoned;
from the moment after the first instant onward, one is also endowed with the past [non-informative action].

In the same way, one who abides in non-restraint is always possessed of the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyāna-saṃvara) with respect to past and future [actions]; however, a noble one (ārya) in the first moment is not possessed of it with respect to the past.
Those two, when established on the noble path in a state of meditative concentration, are conjoined with the present [non-informative action].
If it exists for one who is in an intermediate state, it is first conjoined with the middle [present] period, and thereafter with both time periods.
One who abides in non-restraint is endowed with unwholesome non-informative action, while one who abides in restraint is endowed with wholesome non-informative action,
as long as the force of their faith or affliction persists.
Furthermore, with respect to informative action (*vijñapti*), all those performing it are endowed with the present one;
from the moment after [the first] instant until its relinquishment, they are endowed with the past one, but not with the unborn one.
One is not endowed with past [non-restraint] that is either obscured or unobscured;
non-restraint is misconduct, immorality, action, and the path of action.
One who is neutral and possesses weak volition, while performing an action, is endowed with informative [action] alone;
an noble person (āryapudgala) who has abandoned or not yet produced informative [action] is endowed with non-informative [action].

That which arises from meditative absorption (dhyānaja) is acquired by the very stage of that absorption; the untainted (anāsrava) [discipline] is acquired by that same noble (ārya) [path]; and that called Prātimokṣa is acquired through the communication of others and so forth.
The undertaking of the restraint (saṃvṛti) lasts for as long as one lives or for a day and night;
there is no non-restraint (asaṃvara) for a single day and night, for it is said that it is not undertaken in such a manner.
The fast is to be undertaken from another at dawn, standing in a lowly posture, repeating what is said;
it must have all its components complete, without ornaments, until the end of the night.
The factors of morality, the factor of heedfulness, and the factors of the vows are, respectively, four, one, and three; by these [last three], there is the loss of mindfulness and intoxication.
Others also have the fast, but not for one who has not gone for refuge;
however, the designation "restrained" applies to them upon their undertaking the status of a lay follower (upāsaka), just as it does for a monk (bhikṣu).
If all [lay practitioners] are indeed restrained, how is it that those who perform only a single part of the duties and so forth are described as such?
It is said to be because of their observance of that [precept], just as the degrees of weakness and so forth of the mind are determined.

He who goes for refuge in the three refuges takes refuge in the dharmas that constitute the Buddha and the Saṅgha— namely, the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) and both [those of those in training and those beyond training]— and in nirvāṇa.
Because sexual misconduct is extremely censurable, because it is easy to avoid, and because its non-performance is easily attained,
the acquisition of restraint occurs according to one's undertaking, not with respect to the entire continuum [of beings].
And because of the consequence of false speech when one transgresses any of the precepts,
[the Buddha prohibited] intoxicants alone as a fault of prohibition, in order to guard the others.
The restraint pertaining to the desire realm is acquired with respect to all [three types of action], both [types of persons], and present [factors];
the dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) restraints are acquired with respect to the fundamental [actions] and at all times.
Restraint is [taken] toward all sentient beings; however, it is distinguished by its factors and causes.
Non-restraint, on the other hand, is [taken] toward all [beings], through all factors, but not by way of causes.
Non-restraint is acquired through action or through formal undertaking;
the acquisition of the remaining types of non-informative matter (avijñapti), however, results from the field, the taking up [of a vow], or the absence of respect.
The abandonment of the restraint of the Prātimokṣa occurs through the renunciation of the training, death,
the appearance of both sexual organs, the cutting off of the roots [of merit], and the passing of the night.
Some say [the loss of the vow occurs] by means of a defeat (pātaniya); others say it is through the disappearance of the True Dharma (saddharmāntardhi).
However, the Kashmiris maintain that for one who has committed an offense, both [the vow and the debt] are considered to exist, like wealth and a debt.

Wholesome [attainment] acquired through dhyāna is abandoned by changing levels or by falling away; likewise for that acquired in the formless realms. However, the noble [attainment] is abandoned by the acquisition of a fruit, by refinement, or by falling away.
Non-restraint [is lost] through the acquisition of restraint, death, or the appearance of both sexual organs;
whereas intermediate [restraint] is lost through the interruption of the force, the undertaking, the action, the object, the life-span, or the roots [of merit].
Wholesome non-material [dharmas] belonging to the desire realm are lost through the severance of the roots [of merit] or through rebirth in a higher realm;
however, afflicted non-material [dharmas] are abandoned through the arising of their antidote.
Non-restraint exists among humans, excluding eunuchs, hermaphrodites, and those of the two-fold nature, as well as the inhabitants of Uttarakuru;
likewise for restraint. Furthermore, the three types of discipline exist among gods and humans.
For the gods born in the realms of desire and form, [the acquisition] is born of meditative absorption; furthermore, it is untainted (anāsrava).
This also applies to those in the formless realm, with the exception of those in the intermediate dhyāna and the non-percipient beings.

Action that is secure, insecure, and other than those; wholesome, unwholesome, and other than those; meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable; and the triad beginning with that to be experienced as pleasure.
Wholesome karma in the desire realm is merit; that which arises in the higher realms is immovable.
For in those stages, karma does not waver with respect to its maturation.

Wholesome [karma] up to the third dhyāna is to be experienced as pleasure; beyond that, it is to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure. However, unwholesome [karma] is to be experienced as suffering in this world.
Some maintain that there is also a middle [rebirth] in the lower realms due to the maturation of the intermediate dhyāna;
for it is held that the maturation of these three occurs neither before nor after one another.
The state of being felt (vedanīyatā) is fivefold: by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), association (saṃprayoga), object (ālambana), maturation (vipāka), and manifestation (saṃmukhībhāva).
That [karma] is both determinate and indeterminate; furthermore, the determinate is of three kinds.
Some maintain that karma is fivefold, due to being experienced in the present life and so forth.

Others say there is a fourfold alternative; three [types of karma] project a rebirth-state (nikāya), while in all cases there is a projection of the four [aggregates]. In the hells, however, wholesome [karma] projects in three ways.

A fool who is detached from a certain realm and remains firm there does not create karma to be experienced upon rebirth (upapadyavedanīya) or in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya). Nor does a noble one (ārya) do so; furthermore, even one who is not firm [in detachment] does not create such karma in the desire realm or at the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
The intermediate state projects twenty-two types [of karma] within the realm of desire;
that [karma] has its fruit in the present life, for it constitutes a single homogeneous group.
That which is performed with intense affliction or faith, with continuity,
toward a field of qualities, and that which consists in the killing of one's parents, is determinate.
Action that bears fruit in the present life arises from the excellence of the field and the intention;
likewise, that which is certain regarding its maturation [arises] from absolute detachment from that level.

For those who have emerged from the meditative attainments of cessation (*nirodha*), non-conflict (*araṇā*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the path of seeing (*darśana*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhatphala*),
the fruit of benefit or harm done toward them is experienced immediately.
The ripening of wholesome karma that is free from vitarka is considered to be mental feeling alone;
however, the ripening of unwholesome karma is bodily feeling alone.
The derangement of the mind occurs within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and it arises from the maturation of karma;
it also arises from fear, injury, physical imbalance, and grief, among those in the desire realm who are not inhabitants of Kuru.
The expression "crookedness," "fault," and "impurity" refers to that which arises from deceit, hatred, and passion, respectively.
Furthermore, karma is fourfold according to the distinction of black, white, and so forth.
Impure karma, that which belongs to the realm of form and desire, and pure karma, respectively, are black, white, and both; the outflow-free [karma] leads to their destruction.

The twelvefold volition that exists during the receptivities to the Dharma and during the eight paths of immediate succession in the state of detachment is the action for the destruction of black karma.
The volition in the ninth [path of immediate succession] leads to the destruction of both the black and white [actions];
that which arises in the final path of immediate succession during the detachment from the dhyānas leads to the destruction of the white [action].
Others know that two types of karma are to be experienced in the hells and in the desire realm respectively;
others hold that what is to be abandoned by vision is black, while other karma born of desire is black-and-white.

The three forms of silence (*mauna*) are, respectively, the non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*) actions of body, speech, and mind; the threefold purity (*śauca*) is all three types of good conduct (*sucarita*).
Unwholesome bodily action and so forth are considered the three types of misconduct;
however, covetousness and the rest, though not actions, constitute the threefold mental misconduct.

By the reversal [of the aforementioned], good conduct is established; through the inclusion of the most prominent [factors] therein, ten paths of action are taught as being either wholesome or unwholesome, as appropriate.

The six unwholesome [paths of action] are non-informative; one is of two kinds. For those who perform them, the seven wholesome ones are of two kinds; those born of meditative concentration are non-informative.
The preparatory stages (sāmantaka) are informative (vijñapti), but may or may not be non-informative (avijñapti);
the reverse is true for the subsequent stages (pṛṣṭha). The preliminary application (prayoga), however, arises from the three roots.
Because they arise immediately after those [three], covetousness and the others are born from the three roots;
likewise, the wholesome states, including their preliminary applications and conclusions, are born from non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
The completion of killing, malicious intent, and harsh speech occurs through hatred;
the completion of sexual misconduct with another's wife, covetousness, and taking what is not given occurs through greed.
Wrong view [is abandoned] through delusion; for the remaining [unwholesome roots], it is held that they are abandoned through all three [roots].
Their objective bases are sentient beings and their enjoyments; these are name-and-form and name, respectively.
For one who dies simultaneously with or before [the victim], there is no fundamental [offense], because another basis [for the act] has arisen;
however, in cases such as armies and the like, because they share a single purpose, all are endowed with the offense just like the actual perpetrator.
Taking life is the intentional killing of another without mistake.
Taking what is not given is the appropriation of another's property by means of force or theft.
Sexual misconduct consists of four types, including approaching those who should not be approached.
False speech is the utterance of words by one with a different perception to someone who understands the meaning.
That which is experienced by the eye, the ear, the mind, and by the [other] three [faculties],
is respectively called seen, heard, cognized, and sensed.

Slander is the speech of one with a defiled mind intended to cause division between others. Harsh speech is all unpleasant speech that is defiled. Frivolous chatter is defiled speech that is nonsensical.

Others say that anything else which is afflicted is [unwholesome], like flattery, song, and dance, as well as a false eulogy. Covetousness, however, is the improper longing for the property of others.

Ill-will is hatred toward sentient beings; wrong view is the denial of the wholesome and the unwholesome. For here, these three are paths of action, and together with the other four, they constitute the seven types of karma.

However, the severance of the roots occurs among humans, entirely and gradually, through the false view that denies cause and fruit, which severs the innate roots of merit pertaining to the desire realm.

A woman or a man whose conduct is governed by views severs [the roots]; that is non-possession. Reconnection occurs through longing and the view of existence; here, it does not happen for one who has committed an immediate transgression.
Volition occurs simultaneously with as many as eight unwholesome [mental factors], or with as many as ten wholesome ones; it never occurs with one, eight, or five.
Frivolous speech, harsh speech, and malice exist in two ways in hell;
covetousness and wrong view exist through possession [only]; and three exist among the Kurus.

The seventh [root] exists here [in Kāmadhātu] by way of its own presence; elsewhere, there are ten unwholesome [roots]. However, the three wholesome [roots] exist everywhere, both by way of actual manifestation and by way of possession.

In the formless realms and among the non-percipient beings, seven [faculties] are acquired; in the remaining [realms], they are both acquired and manifested, excluding those in the hells and among the Kurus.
All [actions] are considered to yield the fruit of dominance (*adhipati-phala*), the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
These three fruits arise from causing suffering, killing, and destroying vitality (*ojas*), respectively.

Bodily and vocal action born of greed is categorized separately as wrong livelihood because it is difficult to purify; however, if it is argued that this refers only to that which arises from greed for requisites, that is not so according to the Sūtra.

In the path of abandonment that is with outflows, karma together with its fruit consists of five [factors]; in the stainless [path], it consists of four. Furthermore, any other wholesome or unwholesome karma is with outflows.
Furthermore, the remaining untainted [dharmas] and those that are neutral have three,
four, two, and likewise three [results], respectively, for a wholesome [dharma] such as the virtuous and so forth.
For an unwholesome [state], there are two, three, and four results respectively for the wholesome and so forth;
for an indeterminate [state], these same wholesome and so forth are two, three, and three results respectively.
All past [dharmas] have four results; those of the present likewise have four; those of the future have two middle results; and for the unborn, there are three future results.
Dharmas belonging to one's own level are four [results]; those belonging to other levels are three or two.
For a learner (śaikṣa), the results of a learner’s action and so forth are three; for a non-learner (aśaikṣa) action, however, they are likewise three.
The dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and so forth are one fruit, three fruits, and two fruits [respectively];
for those other than these two, the dharmas of those in training and so forth are two, two, and five fruits [respectively].
Three, four, and one [result] belong to karma to be abandoned by seeing, starting with that [karma];
two, four, and three belong to karma to be abandoned by cultivation.
For that which is not to be abandoned, there are respectively one, two, and four [results].
Some say that what is improperly performed is defiled, as is what deviates from the prescribed rule.
One [karma] projects one birth; many [karmas] are the completers.
The two mindless attainments do not project, nor do acquisitions.
The deeds of immediate retribution, intense afflictions, the miserable destinies, the Kauravas, and the non-percipient beings— these are considered the threefold obscuration.
The immediate [karmas] are held to exist in the three continents; however, they are not admitted for eunuchs and the like.
This is because they provide little assistance and lack a sense of shame. As for the remaining [non-immediate karmas], they exist in all five realms of existence.
Schism in the Saṃgha, however, is a dissociated factor (viprayukta) whose intrinsic nature is disharmony;
it is a non-defiled neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta) dharma, and the Saṃgha is possessed of it.
That schismatic is endowed with that fault of lying;
he is cooked in Avīci for an eon, and his sufferings increase as the [contributing factors] increase.
A monk who has practiced vision and conduct breaks the [Saṃgha], except among fools;
he is broken when he assents to a different path from that of the Teacher, and he does not remain separated for more than one night.
That is considered a schism of the Wheel (cakrabheda) occurring in Jambūdvīpa by nine or more [monks];
it is a schism of action (karmabheda) in the three continents, and that occurs with eight or more [monks].
At the beginning, at the end, before the Arbuda hell, before the [final] age, when the Sage has passed away,
and when the boundary has not been established— the schism of the Wheel does not occur.
Because of the rejection or destruction of one who has been helpful or a field of merit,
even if the mother is disguised by another appearance, she remains the mother from whose blood one is born.
One who intends to strike the Buddha does not incur [the full offense] from the blow itself;
nor can one who has applied himself to an immediate transgression (ānantarya) attain the fruit of detachment (vairāgya).
False speech regarding a schism in the Saṅgha is considered the gravest offense;
in this world, volition directed toward the Peak of Existence is the most fruitful among wholesome actions.
Violating an Arhatī mother, killing one established in certainty, [killing] a Bodhisattva, [killing] a Śaikṣa, and stealing from the means of subsistence of the Saṃgha.
The five actions similar to the immediate [offenses] are: the fifth is the destruction of a stūpa;
these karmas create an extreme obstacle to the attainment of patience, the state of a non-returner, and arhatship.
From what point onward is one a bodhisattva? From the moment one performs the actions that produce the marks [of a Great Being].
[Such a person] is born in a happy realm, of noble birth, with unimpaired faculties, male, remembering former births, and irreversible.
In Jambudvīpa, as a male being, facing [the Buddha] with the intention directed toward a Buddha,
one who has a hundred kalpas remaining projects that [bodhisattva vow] consisting of reflection.
Each [of these] arises from a hundred merits at the end of the three incalculable eons;
they were Vipaśyin, Dīpaṅkara, Ratnaśikhin, and Śākyamuni in the past.
The perfection of giving is fulfilled by one who, out of compassion, gives everything to everyone everywhere;
the perfections of patience and ethical discipline are fulfilled by one who, though still possessing desire, feels no anger even when his limbs are being severed.
Through the hymn to Tiṣya, there is merit; immediately following [the mention of] vigor, wisdom, and concentration, there are action and its basis—this triad is like the paths of action.
That by which something is given, out of a desire to honor or to benefit others, is "giving" (dāna);
it consists of the actions of body and speech along with their motivation, and its fruit is great enjoyment.
A gift is given for one's own benefit, for the benefit of others, for the benefit of both, or for neither of these benefits;
its specific distinctions, moreover, arise from the excellence of the giver, the object, and the field.

The donor is distinguished by faith and other qualities; he gives with respect and so forth. Therefore, there arise: respect, a noble inclination, timeliness, and the attainment of what cannot be taken away.
Through the perfection of color and other qualities, an object becomes beautiful in form or renowned;
from that [perfection], there arises popularity and limbs with a soft touch pleasant according to the season.
A field is distinguished by its state of existence, its suffering, its helpfulness, and its virtues;
the foremost [field] is for one liberated giving to one liberated, and the eighth is for a Bodhisattva.
An immeasurable gift is given even to those who are not noble (anārya) when it is offered to one's mother, father, the sick, a preacher of the Dharma, and a Bodhisattva in their final birth.
The basis, the field, the support, the application, the volition, and the intention—
due to the weakness or intensity of these, there is the weakness or intensity of karma.
Action is said to be accumulated by way of intentionality, completion, absence of regret, the absence of counteractive factors, its retinue, and its maturation.
Merit resulting from relinquishment at a shrine exists even when there is no recipient, just like [the merit of] loving-kindness and so forth;
for even in a bad field, a desirable fruit arises because there is no reversal between the seed and its fruit.
Immorality is unwholesome form; morality is the abstention from it, which is twofold:
from that which is prohibited by the Buddha, and that which is pure, possessing four qualities.
Wholesome [action] that is not destroyed by immorality or its causes, and which relies on its antidote and tranquility, is concentrated; however, it is "cultivation" because it perfumes the mind.
Ethical discipline is primary for attaining heaven; meditative cultivation is for the sake of dissociation.
These four constitute "Brahma-merit" because one rejoices in the heavens for an eon.
The gift of Dharma is the teaching of the sūtras and so forth as they truly are, without affliction.
Wholesome [action] is threefold: that which conduces to merit, to nirvāṇa, and to penetration.
Action set in motion by yoga, together with its originator, is threefold:
writing, seals, calculation, poetry, and arithmetic, respectively.
Faulty, obscured, and inferior phenomena are afflicted; pure and stainless phenomena are sublime.
Conditioned wholesome phenomena are to be cultivated, but liberation is unsurpassed.
Thus ends the fourth treasury-location (kośasthāna) of the Abhidharmakośa, titled "Exposition of Karma" (Karmanirdeśa).
The Fifth Treasury-Locality.
Om, homage to the Buddha!
The root of existence are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): attachment, and likewise aversion;
Furthermore, these are pride, ignorance, views, and doubt. (VAkK 5.1)
Due to the division of the six types of attachment, seven are taught; attachment to existence arises from two realms.
Because it is inward-looking, it was established separately in order to exclude the notion that it is liberation.

The views are fivefold: the view of a self-identity, false view, the view of grasping at extremes, and the two forms of adherence—adherence to views and adherence to rules and rituals; thus, there are ten [factors].
These ten, seven, seven, and eight [defilements], excluding those abandoned by the three and two views respectively,
are abandoned in the desire realm through the vision of suffering and the other truths in their proper order.
The four [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation are likewise non-obstructive in the realm of form and similarly in the formless realm; thus, ninety-eight [afflictions] are recognized.

Those born of the peak of existence (bhavāgra) that are to be destroyed by patience (kṣānti) are abandoned by insight (dṛgheya) alone; those born of the remaining [stages] that are not to be destroyed by patience are abandoned by both insight and cultivation (bhāvanā), but those not to be destroyed by patience are abandoned by cultivation alone.

The views of self and what belongs to self, eternalism and nihilism, and the views of non-existence, inferiority, and superiority; the view regarding what is not a cause and what is not the path—these are the five views.
Because it proceeds from the perversion of regarding the Lord and so forth as an eternal self,
the adherence to [them] as causes is to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering.
From three views, the four perversions arise by way of inversion; through investigation and superimposition, while perception and mind follow their lead.
The seven types of pride are ninefold; they arise from the three [roots] and are abandoned through vision and cultivation.
Likewise, the outbursts such as killing are to be abandoned through cultivation.
In an Arya, the desire for existence does not arise, nor do [the views] such as "it exists" (vidhi) and so forth;
nor does the conceit "I am" (asmitā), because it is nourished by [wrong] views; nor is there unwholesome regret (kaukṛtya).
The views to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause are universal,
as are doubt together with them, and that ignorance which is unique.
Of these, nine have the upper realms as their object, excluding two views;
those that coexist with them, excluding acquisitions, are also omnipresent.
False view and doubt, as well as ignorance associated with them and independent ignorance, are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path; these six have the untainted as their object.

The path that is the cessation of one's own level consists of six levels; the path belonging to nine levels is the object of those [cognitions] whose range it is, for paths are indeed mutually causal.
He has no attachment because it is something to be abandoned; no aversion because there is no harm done;
no pride and no two types of misapprehension, because of his state of peace, purity, and supremacy.
The universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere to their entire [level];
the non-universal ones adhere to their own category within their own level by way of their object.
Those [defilements] do not have the outflows of a higher realm as their object, because they are not appropriated and because they are opposed to them;
however, whichever [defilement] is associated with whatever [object], it [is defiled] in that [object] through association.

All [factors] in the higher realms are neutral; in the desire realm, the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes, and the ignorance associated with these two are neutral, while the remaining factors here are unwholesome.
In the realm of desire, the unwholesome roots are attachment, aversion, and delusion.
There are three unwholesome roots: craving, ignorance, and that [same] cognition.
