Because they function in two ways and extend upward, there are no others besides these; thus, according to the outsiders (Bāhyakas), there are only four—namely, craving, views, pride, and delusion—due to the three types of meditators being associated with ignorance.

The answer is by way of a categorical declaration, by way of analysis, by way of counter-questioning, and by way of setting aside—just as in the cases of death, birth, excellence, and the identity or difference of the self. (AK 5.22)
One is bound to an object by attachment, aversion, and pride when these have arisen and are present in the past or the present, provided they have not been abandoned.
One is bound everywhere by these future mental [factors]; by others belonging to their own time-period;
by those that are unborn, one is bound everywhere; and by all the remaining ones, one is bound everywhere.
Because existence in all three times has been taught, because of the two, because of the real object, and because of the fruit—
those who assert the existence of that [past and future] are accepted as Sarvāstivādins, and they are of four kinds.
These are designated as the "alteration of state," the "alteration of characteristic," and the "alteration of position.
The third [position] is the best: the time periods are established by way of their activity (*kāritra*).

What is the obstacle? Why is it not otherwise? For one who exists thus, there is no connection with the [three] time periods. By what means are there the states of being unborn and destroyed? Profound indeed is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
When that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering has been abandoned, one is bound by all the universal [defilements] remaining;
and when a previous category has been abandoned, one is bound by the remaining defilements that have those as their object.
Those [factors] born in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, by the vision of its cause, and by cultivation,
are the objects of the three types of their own [realm's] consciousness, of one type of consciousness belonging to the form realm, and of the stainless (amala) consciousness.
Those born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) are the objects of their own [level], the three lower levels, one higher level, and the pure (amala).
Those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are the objects of the three types of consciousness belonging to each of the three realms and the untainted (anāsrava).
All [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have as their objects those [factors] belonging to their own level and higher levels.
The untainted [factors] are of three kinds; they are the objects of the last three [categories of consciousness] within the three realms and of the untainted [consciousness].
That which is with latent dispositions (sānuśaya) is of two kinds: afflicted and non-afflicted; [the former] is so because of the latent dispositions that follow along.
From delusion comes doubt, from that comes false view, and from that comes the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
From that [view of self] comes the adherence to extremes; from that, the clinging to rules and rituals;
from that, the [wrong] views; then passion for one's own view, pride, and hatred toward others—this is the sequence.
From an unabandoned latent disposition (*anuśaya*), from an object that has presented itself,
and from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), the affliction (*kleśa*) arises with its causes complete.
In the realm of desire, the defilements (kleśa) accompanied by their active outbursts (paryavasthāna), excluding delusion (moha), constitute the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava);
in the realms of form and formlessness, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) alone constitute the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava).
For those [factors] belonging to the stage of meditative concentration are indeterminate and inwardly directed;
therefore, they are grouped together as "ignorance," which constitutes a separate outflow (āsrava).
Likewise, the floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga) include the views; however, they are treated separately because of their intensity.
They are not included among the outflows (āsava), for it is said that when they are without companions, they do not conform to the nature of an outflow.

That very ignorance as previously described is divided into two types by distinguishing it from views; the appropriations consist of these two, while ignorance is mixed with them because it is not itself a grasper.
These are called "proclivities" (anuśaya) because they are subtle, because they adhere, because they increase in two ways, and because they bind one continuously.
They cause one to dwell, they flow forth, they carry away, they adhere, and they grasp; such are the etymological definitions of these [defilements] as "outflows" (āsrava) and so forth.
Furthermore, they are taught as fivefold according to the distinctions of fetters (saṃyojana) and so forth;
because of the commonality of their substantial nature and their mode of grasping, the two views constitute a single separate fetter.
Because envy and avarice are exclusively unwholesome and because both are independent, they are taught among these [fetters] as two separate fetters.
The five lower fetters are of two kinds; by two of them there is no transcending of the desire realm, but by three there is returning again. The triad is grasped by way of the gate and the root.
The desire not to go, confusion regarding the path, and doubt about the path—these are the obstacles to proceeding toward liberation; therefore, there is the teaching of these three.

The higher-tier fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya) are likewise fivefold: the two types of attachment arising from the form and formless realms, as well as restlessness, pride, and delusion; and through the power of views, there are three bonds (bandhana).

Those other afflicted mental factors included in the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) which are distinct from the primary afflictions (kleśa) are also secondary afflictions (upakleśa), yet they are not designated by the term "affliction."
Lack of shame, lack of dread, envy, avarice, restlessness, remorse, lethargy, and torpor: these are the eight types of envelopments (paryavasthāna).
Anger and concealment arise from attachment; lack of shame, restlessness, and avarice [also arise from attachment].
Dispute arises from concealment; lethargy, torpor, and lack of moral dread arise from ignorance.
Remorse arises from doubt; anger and envy follow from aversion.
Furthermore, there are six other stains of the afflictions: deceit, guile, and likewise pride.
Malice and enmity are born of attachment; deceit and arrogance are born of hatred, as are enmity and harmfulness.
From the adherence to views arises spite; deceit is born from views.
Among these, lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, torpor, and restlessness are twofold.
The others are to be abandoned by cultivation, as are the independent afflictions (svatantra-mala).
In the desire realm, the three unwholesome [roots] are of two types; beyond that, they are indeterminate.
Deceit and guile exist in the first two dhyānas because they deceive Brahmā;
lethargy, restlessness, and pride exist in the three realms; the others arise only in the desire realm.

Those secondary afflictions that are abandoned by insight, which are co-existent with the [root] afflictions, and which belong to the level of mental consciousness, as well as those that are independent—these six have the mental consciousness as their basis; others have all six consciousnesses as their basis.
For attachment is associated with the two [feelings of] pleasure; aversion is the opposite;
delusion is associated with all [feelings]; and false view, however, is associated with mental suffering and pleasure.
Doubt arises with mental dissatisfaction; others arise with mental satisfaction born of desire.
All [of these] also arise with equanimity; those belonging to higher stages arise with their own respective [factors] according to their level.
Regret, envy, anger, harmfulness, enmity, and resentment are associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*); however, avarice is the opposite.
Deceit, guile, and hypocrisy; torpor is associated with both [types of feeling];
intoxication with both pleasant ones; all [mental factors] are associated with equanimity; and the other four are associated with five [feelings].

In the realm of desire, the hindrances are five because they share a single antidote, a single nourishment, and a single function; and because two of them have a single leader, due to their destruction of the aggregates and their nature as doubt.
Through the full understanding of the object, through the destruction of that which has it as its object,
through the abandonment of the object, and through the arising of the antidote, there is cessation.

The counteragent is considered to be fourfold— consisting of abandonment, support, the state of being, and that which is called "corruption"— and the affliction to be abandoned is held to be [abandoned] by means of its object.

Remoteness is of four kinds: due to difference in nature, due to being an opposing factor, due to spatial separation, and due to time—just as, for example, there is remoteness between the elements, moral discipline, different locations, and the two time periods.

The destruction [of the defilements] occurs once; however, the attainment of disjunction from them occurs again and again during the arising of the counteragent, the acquisition of the fruit, and the refinement of the faculties.
Full comprehension consists of nine types: the destruction of two categories of the desire realm and so forth;
one [comprehension] occurs upon the destruction of two [categories], and there are two [more] for those above; likewise, there are exactly three of them.

The other three thorough knowledges (parijñā) consist of the destruction of the lower fetters, the destruction of the outflows regarding form, and the destruction of all outflows; six are the fruit of the receptivities (kṣānti), while the remainder are the fruit of knowledge (jñāna).

The fruit of the *anāgamya* stage consists of all [the fruits]; for the [four] dhyānas, there are five or eight; for one preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and for the three fundamental formless attainments (*maulārūpya*), there is one.
All [the knowledges] belong to the Noble Path; two belong to the worldly path;
three belong to subsequent knowledge; six belong to dharma-knowledge; and five belong to its side.
Full comprehension [is attained] through the acquisition of the outflow-free disconnection, through the mutilation of the peak of existence,
through the eradication of the two causes, and through the transcendence of the realm.
One established in the path of seeing is endowed with either one or up to five [knowledges];
one established in the path of cultivation, however, is endowed with six, or with one, or with two.
Their total number is determined by the attainment of detachment from the realms and the fruits [of the path]:
one, two, five, or six; some abandon them, while no one attains all five.
The discussion concerning full comprehension is concluded.
The fifth treasury-location (kośasthāna) of the Abhidharmakośa, titled "Exposition of the Latent Dispositions" (anuśayanirdeśa), is completed.
Whatever merit is herein from Śrī Lāmāvāka— this is the sixth treasury-location (kośasthāna). Om, homage to the Buddha!
The abandonment of the afflictions is said to result from the vision and cultivation of the truths.
The path of cultivation is twofold, but that which is called the path of vision is untainted (anāsrava).
The four truths have been stated: suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path; their sequence follows the order of their realization.
Pleasant, unpleasant, and those other than these— all contaminated phenomena— are suffering in their entirety, according to their respective connection with the three types of suffering.

That which, when broken, no longer evokes its own cognition, and that which, when other [factors] are excluded by the mind, no longer evokes its own cognition—like a jar or water—is conventionally real; otherwise, it is ultimately real.
Established in moral conduct and possessing [the wisdoms of] hearing and reflection, one applies oneself to cultivation.
The cognitions consisting of hearing and so forth have as their objects the name, both [name and meaning], and the meaning.
These belong to one who possesses the two types of withdrawal, not to one who is discontented or has great desires.
Contentment is the lack of longing for more regarding what has been obtained; great desire is the longing for what has not yet been obtained.
Their opposites are the antidotes to those perversions; they belong to the three realms and are also pure.
They consist of non-attachment, as do the noble lineages, three of which have contentment as their essence.

Livelihood is established by three [precepts] through the final precept; this is for the sake of opposing the arising of craving, and for the temporary and ultimate pacification of the desire for things associated with the notions of "mine" and "I."
Entry into that [meditative state] is by means of the meditation on the foul and mindfulness of breathing;
for those with excessive passion and discursive thought, it is by means of the skeleton for all who possess passion.
The beginner is so called because of the expansion and contraction of the visualization of bones as far as the ocean;
one who has achieved mastery is said to have abandoned [the visualization] from the bone of the foot up to half of the skull.

The "transcended mental application" [meditation] consists of fixing the mind between the eyebrows. Non-greed is its nature; it belongs to ten stages, takes the visible objects of the desire realm as its object, and arises in human beings. It is the meditation on the foul.

Mindfulness of breathing is wisdom; it belongs to five stages, has wind as its object, and is based in the desire realm. It does not exist among outsiders and is of six kinds, beginning with counting.

In-breathing and out-breathing are dependent on the body; they are designated as belonging to sentient beings, are non-appropriated, and are of the nature of outflow. Furthermore, these two are not perceived by a mind of a lower stage.
One who has accomplished calm abiding (śamatha) should practice the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) by examining the body,
feelings, mind, and phenomena through their two characteristics.

Wisdom consists of hearing and so forth; others [the remaining three] have association and objects as their nature. Their order is according to their arising, while the tetrad is established as the antidote to the perversions.
Established in the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena with all things as its object,
he contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
From that, the arising of the "Heat" stage occurs; it has the four truths as its object and consists of sixteen aspects. From the Heats, the "Summits" arise; they are likewise of the same nature.
The production of both [the patience and the knowledge] occurs through the Dharma; however, their increase occurs through others as well.
From those [knowledges], patience arises in two ways; likewise, its increase occurs through the Dharma.

But the highest [degree] has as its object the suffering pertaining to the desire realm, and it lasts for only one moment; likewise are the supreme mundane dharmas. All of these, however, consist of the five aggregates, excluding acquisitions.
Thus, the aids to penetration are fourfold and consist of cultivation;
they belong to the stages of the threshold, the intermediate, and the dhyānas, or alternatively, two of them also belong to the lower stages.
A woman attains the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharma) based on two supports;
the noble one abandons them by relinquishing the stage (bhūmi), whereas the non-noble one abandons them through death.
The first two [results] are also lost through falling away; there, the vision of the truths occurs from the fundamental [meditative state].
When those [attainments] are lost, there is the acquisition of what was not previously obtained; the two types of loss consist in non-possession.
One who has attained the "summit" does not sever the roots [of virtue]; one who has attained "patience" does not go to the miserable states.
Having turned away from the lineage of the disciples, two may become Buddhas, while three may become the other [Pratyekabuddhas].
For both the Teacher and the Rhinoceros-like [Pratyekabuddha], everything up to enlightenment occurs in a single sitting in the final dhyāna.
Prior to those [nirvedhabhāgīyas] is the stage conducive to liberation; liberation is attained quickly within three existences.
The three types of action consisting of hearing and reflection are projected among humans;
from the supreme mundane dharmas, the untainted receptivity to the dharma arises.
Then, regarding the suffering of the desire realm, there is likewise the dharma-knowledge;
and again, regarding the remaining suffering, there are the subsequent patience and knowledge; and it is the same for the other three truths.
Thus, this realization of the truths consists of sixteen moments of consciousness and is threefold—
known as the vision, the object, and the task— and it belongs to the same stage as the supreme mundane dharmas.
The patiences and knowledges are, respectively, the uninterrupted paths and the paths of liberation.
Because of seeing what was not previously seen, fifteen moments therein constitute the path of seeing.
Among them, those with dull and sharp faculties are the followers by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the followers by dharma (dharmānusārin);
they have not yet abandoned what is to be abandoned by cultivation, and they are candidates for the first fruit.
Up until the destruction of five types [of afflictions], they are candidates for the second fruit;
having abandoned [the remaining] nine, or being detached from the desire realm or above, they are candidates for the third fruit.
In the sixteenth moment, however, those two who were candidates [in the preceding moments] become established in the fruit;
at that time, they are respectively those who have attained through faith and those who have attained through vision, being of dull and sharp faculties.
Therefore, while abiding in a fruit, there is no attainment of a path superior to that fruit;
thus, one who abides in a fruit is not a candidate for the next stage unless they apply themselves toward excellence.
For there are nine types of defects and likewise nine types of qualities on each stage,
due to the further division of the weak, medium, and intense into [weak-weak], and so forth.
One who abides in the fruit [of stream-entry] and has not yet exhausted the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation is "one who is limited to seven births at most.
One who is liberated from three or four categories [of defilements] is "one who goes from family to family," having two or three more births remaining.
One who has destroyed up to the fifth category [of afflictions] is a candidate for the second fruit;
however, one who has exhausted the sixth category is a once-returner.
Having exhausted seven or eight portions of the defilements, he is one who has only one birth remaining (ekajanman) or one who is separated from nirvāṇa by a single interval (ekavīcika);
he is also one who has entered upon the third fruit, and he becomes a non-returner (anāgāmin) through the destruction of the nine [remaining] defilements.
He is one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion or without exertion in the intermediate state;
he is also one who goes upstream, having practiced the mixed meditations, and goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
He is a leaper, a half-leaper, one who dies everywhere, or another who goes to the peak of existence;
another who goes to the formless realm is of four kinds, while yet another attains nirvana here.
Furthermore, by dividing each of the three [realms] into three types, nine [classes] of those who have attained the form realm are taught;
their further distinctions arise from differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties.
The seven good destinies are considered to be [subdivisions of] the upward-streamer (ūrdhvasrotas) by way of their non-distinction;
they are so designated because of their engagement in good and bad conduct, and because of having gone without returning.
A noble one who has not undergone a change of birth and has gone to another realm within the desire realm,
as well as one born in a higher realm, does not possess the capacity for the transformation of faculties or for falling away.
The fourth [dhyāna] is first interspersed before its final accomplishment through the mixing of moments;
this is for the sake of rebirth, for dwelling [in meditative ease], and also out of fear of the afflictions.
Because that [attainment] is fivefold, there are exactly five rebirths in the Pure Abodes.
Furthermore, one who has attained cessation is considered a non-returner who is a body-witness.
One who has abandoned up to the eighth part of the peak of existence is a candidate for arhatship;
and in the ninth path of immediate succession, he is one whose concentration is like a diamond.
Through the attainment of that destruction, there arises the knowledge of destruction; at that time, he is an Arhat beyond training.
Detachment from the peak of existence is achieved through the supramundane path; from other levels, it is achieved in two ways.

Regarding the attainment of dissociation from defilements through noble detachment, some say it is twofold— both by the mundane and the supramundane— because when [the mundane path] is abandoned, there is no longer possession of the afflictions.
One who is partially liberated from the Peak of Existence possesses non-possession [of the lower stages] like one born in a higher realm;
through the untainted Anāgamya, there is detachment from all [stages].
In the conquest of the three realms, the final path of liberation arises either from a dhyāna or its preparatory stage (sāmantaka); it does not arise from a preparatory stage for the higher [realms].
Through the eight noble paths, there is the conquest of one's own realm and the realm above.
The worldly paths of immediate succession and liberation have, respectively, the aspects of "calm" and so forth, or "gross" and so forth; their objects are the higher and lower realms.

If he is immovable, the knowledge of non-arising follows from the knowledge of destruction; if not, then for every Arhat, that [knowledge of destruction] is either the knowledge of destruction or the vision of one beyond training.
The state of a recluse (śrāmaṇya) is the stainless path; its fruit is both conditioned and unconditioned.
These consist of eighty-nine [moments]: the paths of liberation together with the cessations.
The establishment of the four fruits occurs due to the presence of five causes:
the abandonment of the previous [path], the attainment of another path, and the aggregation of cessations within the fruit.
Then there is the acquisition of the eight knowledges and the cultivation of the sixteen aspects;
however, because it is mixed with what is worldly, the attainment of the untainted is the fruit of steadfastness.
That very same [path] is called the "Brahminhood" and the "Wheel of Brahmā" because it proceeds as Brahmā;
however, it is the "Wheel of Dharma" because it is the path of vision (dṛṅmārga), due to its swift movement and its possession of spokes and so forth.
The attainment of the last [fruit] occurs in all three realms; however, it does not occur above [the desire realm], because the path of vision does not exist there.
Furthermore, according to scripture, this [attainment] is of two kinds here [in the desire realm] due to the absence of spiritual urgency, whereas there [in the higher realms] it is the final one.
Six types of Arhats are recognized; among them, five arise from those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta).
Their liberation is occasional (sāmayikī); for the one of immovable nature (akopyadharman), it is unshakable (akopyā).
Therefore, he is one liberated at any time, and he belongs to the lineage of those who have attained vision;
some belong to that lineage from the very beginning, while others have arrived there through refinement.
The falling away from four [fruits] occurs from their lineage; the falling away from five occurs from the fruit, but not from the previous one.
Śaikṣas and non-noble ones possess six lineages; there is no transition [of lineage] in the path of seeing.
Falling away is to be known as threefold: from what has been attained, from what has not yet been attained, and from enjoyment.
The last [type] applies to the Teacher; the middle to the unshakable one; but for others, all three types apply.
One who has fallen from the fruit does not die [in that state], nor does he perform an improper act;
for in the case of the immovable [arhat], there are nine paths of liberation and nine paths of immediate retribution due to excessive cultivation.
In the state of being attained through vision, each [indriya] is untainted (anāsrava); their increase occurs among humans.
The one beyond training (aśaikṣa) relies on nine stages, whereas the one in training (śaikṣa) relies on six, because of this.
Having abandoned the fruit along with its specific qualities, one attains the [next] fruit by increasing [the faculties].
These two types of Buddhas and seven types of Śrāvakas—these nine possess ninefold faculties.
The seven types of persons are established by way of application, faculties, meditative attainments, liberation, and both; yet these are six, because there are two each in the three paths.
One who has attained cessation is "liberated in both ways"; the other is liberated by wisdom.
A learner is said to be "complete" when perfected in meditative attainments, faculties, and fruits.
The perfection of one beyond training is twofold; in brief, the path is fourfold, known as preparation, uninterrupted [path], liberation, and excellence.
The path within the dhyānas is the easy practice; it is difficult on other stages.
For one of dull faculties, the higher knowledges are slow; for the other, however, they are swift.

Enlightenment consists of the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising; because they are conducive to that [enlightenment], the thirty-seven factors are its wings. By name there are thirty-seven, but substantially there are ten.
Faith, vigor, mindfulness, wisdom, concentration, joy, equanimity, pliancy, morality, and intention; for the foundations of mindfulness are indeed wisdom.
Vigor is called the right exertions, and the bases of psychic power are concentrations;
these names are used by taking the primary factors, yet all these qualities are indeed preparatory.
The seven groups are manifested respectively in the stages of the beginner, the aids to penetration, cultivation, and seeing.
The factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path are untainted; the others are of two kinds.
All are present in the first dhyāna; in the preparatory stage (anāgamya), they are present except for joy.
In the second [dhyāna], they exist except for resolve; in the first two, they are devoid of those two;
in the intermediate dhyāna, they are present along with the limbs of morality; and in the three formless [attainments], they are present along with those two.
In the desire realm and at the peak of existence, the factors of enlightenment and the limbs of the path are excluded;
likewise, upon the vision of the [first] three truths, the two types of verified confidence—confidence in the precepts and confidence in the Dharma—are excluded.
Upon the clear realization of the Path, there is also the acquisition of the Buddha and his Saṅgha;
the Dharma consists of the three truths for the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas.
As for the path, in terms of substantial entities, there are two: stainless faith and ethical discipline.
Liberation is not stated to be a limb of the learner because he is still bound; furthermore, that [liberation] is of two kinds.
The unconditioned [liberation] is the abandonment of the afflictions, while the conditioned [liberation] is resolute confidence (adhimukti).
That very [conditioned liberation], together with its factors, constitutes the two types of liberation; wisdom, as previously described, is enlightenment (bodhi).
The mind of one who is being born as an adept (aśaikṣa) is liberated from its obscuration;
however, the path that is ceasing abandons that very obscuration.
The unconditioned element is called detachment, which is the destruction of passion;
it is the element of abandonment for others, while that which is called cessation pertains to the objective entity.

One becomes weary through the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its cause; one becomes detached through all those [patiences and knowledges] by which [one abandons]. Thus, there arises a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
Thus ends the sixth treasury-location of the Abhidharmakośa, titled "The Exposition of the Path and the Persons."
The Seventh Treasury-Locus.
Homage to the Buddha.
The stainless patiences are not knowledge; the cognitions of destruction and non-arising are not vision;
noble cognition other than those is both; all others are knowledge, and six are also vision.

Knowledge is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava). The first is the conventional (saṃvṛti) knower; the knowledge without outflows is of two kinds: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).

Conventional knowledge has all things as its object; that which is called the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has the suffering and so forth of the desire realm as its object; whereas subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) has the suffering and so forth of the higher realms as its object.
These same two, through the distinction of the truths, constitute these four;
furthermore, those two are the knowledge of non-arising and the knowledge of destruction, which were mentioned first.
In the subsequent knowledge of the cause of suffering, the knowledge of another's mind arises from four [knowledges];
however, it does not know that [mind] which has transcended the stages, the faculties, or the persons, nor that which is past or unborn.
A Śrāvaka knows two moments of vision—one belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge and the other to the category of subsequent knowledge—mutually;
a Pratyekabuddha knows three; and a Buddha knows all of them without effort.
For the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) is the certainty regarding the truths that they have been fully known and so forth;
the cognition of non-arising (anutpādamati) is considered to be [the certainty] that there is nothing further to be fully known, and so on.

There are ten [types of knowledge] by way of intrinsic nature and antidote, by way of aspect and the object of the aspect, and by way of application, having accomplished the task, and the accumulation of causes.

That which is the knowledge of dharma regarding cessation or the path on the path of cultivation is the antidote to all three realms; however, that which pertains to the desire realm is not subsequent knowledge.
Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have sixteen aspects; otherwise, conventional knowledge is likewise fourfold, each according to its own respective aspects of the truths.
Likewise, the supreme mental consciousness— both stainless and with stains—
has as its aspect the specific characteristic of the object of knowledge and has each individual substance as its domain.
The remaining [knowledge] has fourteen aspects, excluding emptiness and non-self;
there is no aspect other than these sixteen that is stainless, according to the treatise.
In substance, there are sixteen aspects; the aspect of wisdom, together with them, constitutes the aspects.
Those [mental states] that possess an object aspect things, but everything that exists is what is aspected.
The first [knowledge] is of three kinds; the others are wholesome. The first exists in all stages;
that called "Dharma" exists in six, and likewise the one called "Subsequent" exists in nine, each being of six kinds.
The knowledge of others' minds within the dhyānas has its basis in the desire and form realms;
however, that which is called the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has its basis in the desire realm, while the other [knowledges] have their basis in all three realms.

The knowledge of cessation is one foundation of mindfulness; the knowledge of others' minds consists of three; the remaining [knowledges] consist of four; and nine have the knowledge of phenomena as their object.
Nine [factors] pertain to the knowledge of the path and its subsequent knowledge; two pertain to the knowledge of suffering and its cause;
ten pertain to four [knowledges]; none pertain to one; furthermore, ten factors are to be applied [to these].
The dharmas of the three realms that are untainted, as well as the unconditioned, are each of two kinds;
one should know that conventional reality, which is other than its own group, is non-self.
One who possesses desire, when endowed with a single cognition, has [one] in the first untainted moment;
in the second, [he has] three; but one situated above [the Desire Realm] increases by one in each of the four [moments].
In the path of seeing, the patiences and knowledges are cultivated as they arise;
therein, future ones of the same type are cultivated, as well as the conventional knowledge during the three subsequent knowledges.
Therefore, that which is called the final [moment] of clear realization possesses the nature of non-arising;
regarding the cessation of its own level and lower levels, it is the last [moment], characterized by the aspects of its own truth, and is produced through effort.
In the sixteenth [moment], there is the cultivation of six for one who is still subject to passion, but seven for one who is free from passion;
on the path of cultivation while still subject to passion, there is that, and above that, the cultivation of seven.

In the uninterrupted paths during the conquest of the seven stages, the acquisition of the superknowledges (abhijñā), and the attainment of the unshakable state; and also in the eight paths of liberation that follow.
In the liberation through the refinement of the trainee's faculties, there is the cultivation of six or seven knowledges;
likewise in the uninterrupted path for the conquest of the peak of existence, there is the cultivation of six.
In the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) of the nine [categories of defilements], ten [faculties] are cultivated for one who is immovable (akopyadharman);
in the transition thereto and in the final liberation, eight are cultivated as previously stated.
That which is cultivated for the sake of detachment from a certain level, as well as that which is acquired on that level and on the lower levels, is cultivated;
however, among the contaminated dharmas, those previously attained are not cultivated at the moment of the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna).
The cultivation of wholesome conditioned phenomena is called "cultivation by acquisition" and "cultivation by practice";
however, for that which is with outflows, there are also "cultivation as an antidote" and "cultivation by elimination."
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) consist of the powers and so forth:
there are ten knowledges regarding what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna), eight regarding the ripening of karma (karmaphala), and nine regarding the meditative absorptions and so forth.
In the case of the resolve regarding the meditations and so forth, the sense faculties, and the realms, as well as in the paths, there are ten conventional knowledges;
in two cases, there are six or ten knowledges of destruction.
The power of the recollection of former abodes, the power of death and rebirth, and the powers of meditative absorptions are established;
the remainder exist on all stages. For what reason is his power unimpeded? Because of this [reason].
The body possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa; in other joints, it is ten times greater.
It is the strength of the sevenfold series beginning with the elephant, and it is the sphere of the tangible.
The four kinds of fearlessness correspond respectively to the first and tenth powers, as well as to the second and seventh; these three consist of mindfulness and wisdom.
Great compassion is conventional wisdom; it differs in eight ways through its equipment, aspects, and objects, as well as through its equality and its intensity.
All Buddhas are equal by virtue of their accumulations, their Dharma-body, and their service for the sake of the world; they are not equal in terms of lifespan, caste, or physical stature.

Other qualities, such as the absence of conflict (araṇā), the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna), the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), and so forth, are shared by disciples and ordinary worldlings alike.
Conventional knowledge and the *araṇā* absorption belong to one of unshakable nature in the final dhyāna;
they are born of humans and have as their object the defilements belonging to the desire realm that have not yet arisen, along with their bases.
In the same way, the knowledge resulting from resolution has everything as its object;
likewise, there are the analytical knowledges (saṃvid) regarding phenomena, their meaning, etymological definitions, and eloquence.
The first three names refer respectively to speech, knowledge, and the irreversible [state];
the fourth refers to mastery over both joined and detached expression and over the path.
This [knowledge] has speech and the path as its objects; it consists of nine knowledges and belongs to all stages.
The analytical knowledge of meaning consists of ten or six knowledges and exists everywhere; the others, however, are conventional knowledge.

The analytical knowledges (dharmapratisaṃvid) exist in the desire realm and the dhyānas; those regarding speech exist in the first dhyāna and the desire realm. One who lacks these [analytical knowledges] does not possess them. These six are the ultimate limits (prāntakoṭika).
That [knowledge] is of six kinds, conforms to all stages, and has reached the culmination of increase; furthermore, for one other than a Buddha, it arises from application.

The supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) consist of the realization through direct experience (sākṣātkriyā) of the knowledge of psychic powers, the divine ear, the minds of others, former births, death and rebirth, and the destruction [of the outflows]; they are sixfold and constitute the wisdom of the path to liberation.
The four [knowledges] are conventional knowledge; the knowledge of another's mind consists of five knowledges.
The supernormal knowledge of the destruction [of the outflows], like the power, exists in the five [factors] within the four dhyānas.
Those [knowledges] whose objects are their own level or a lower level are obtained through detachment; however, they are appropriate [only for those on higher levels].
The third consists of three applications of mindfulness; the first consists of the divine ear and the divine eye.
The supernormal powers of the ear and the eye are neutral; the others are wholesome.
Three are "knowledges" (vidyā) because they eliminate ignorance regarding the past limit and so forth.
The last two [knowledges] belong to one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and are called by that name because they arise within their continuum;
they are accepted as belonging to a learner (śaikṣa), but they are not called "sciences" (vidyā) because the continuum of one still possessed of ignorance (sāvidya) persists.
The first, the third, and the sixth are the miracles of instruction;
they are supreme because they are unerring and because they connect [beings] with what is beneficial and desired results.

Supernormal power (ṛddhi) is meditative concentration (samādhi); it consists of going and transformation. The movement of the Teacher is "swift as thought" (manojavā), while for others it is also "carried" (vāhinī) or "by resolve" (ādhimokṣikī). These are the three types of movement.
The external emanations belonging to the desire realm consist of four sense-bases and are of two kinds;
those belonging to the form realm consist of two. These [emanations] are produced by fourteen types of emanation-minds.
In order, the fruits of the dhyānas range from two up to five; they do not arise from a higher stage.
Their acquisition is like that of the dhyānas themselves: from the pure [dhyāna] and from its own [level]; and from those [fruits], those [pure dhyānas] also arise.
Emanation occurs by means of [the mind] belonging to its own level, but speech also by means of that belonging to a lower level;
however, for one who is not a Teacher, it is only together with the emanator, because it proceeds through the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of another.
Even for one who has died, there is empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), but not for one who is unstable; however, others say it does not exist [for the dead].
At first, one [empowerment] is performed by many; but once it has been mastered, it is the reverse.
The indeterminate [mind] born of cultivation is of three kinds, while that born of rebirth is likewise;
furthermore, it is fivefold when including those produced by supernatural power, by spells, by herbs, and by karma.
The divine ear and eye are translucent matter belonging to the stages of meditative absorption;
they are always homogeneous and unimpaired, having as their objects that which is distant, subtle, and so forth.
Since the fleshly eye does not perceive forms that are distant, obscured, or subtle, nor those that are all-pervading,
the divine eye is therefore desired.
Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas see respectively two thousand, three thousand, and innumerable world-systems.
Whatever else is obtained through rebirth is visible to them; however, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not.
But that knowledge of others' minds is of three kinds: that produced by reasoning, that produced by spells, and that which is innate;
among these, hell-beings know it at the beginning, whereas humans do not possess it as something acquired at birth.
The seventh treasury-location (kośasthāna) of the Abhidharmakośa, titled "Exposition of Knowledge" (jñānanirdeśa).
The Eighth Chapter of the Treasury.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
The four meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are said to be twofold: their states of rebirth and meditative attainment (samāpatti).
Meditative attainment is virtuous one-pointedness of mind; together with its attendants, it consists of the five aggregates.
Possessing investigation, joy, and bliss, each successive [dhyāna] is devoid of the preceding factors;
likewise, the formless attainments consist of four aggregates and are born from seclusion from the lower stages.

Those known as the "perceptions of attenuated form," together with the three preparatory stages, do not possess the existence of form within the formless realm; rather, the arising of form [there] proceeds from the mind.
Those named Infinite Space, Infinite Consciousness, and Nothingness arise from such application;
however, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception arises because of dullness.
Thus, the fundamental substance of attainment is of eight kinds and three types:
seven are associated with tasting, pure, and untainted; the eighth is of two types.
That which is associated with relishing is mundane wholesomeness accompanied by craving;
that which is to be relished is the pure [wholesome] state, while the supramundane is untainted.
In the first [dhyāna], there are the five: applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and concentration (samādhi).
In the second, there is a fourfold set of factors: joy and the others [bliss and concentration], as well as inner serenity (prasāda).
In the third [dhyāna], there are five: equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and stability.
At the end [the fourth dhyāna], there are four: neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, mindfulness, and concentration.
In substance, there are eleven: serenity and pleasure in the first two [dhyānas];
clarity is faith; and joy is mental happiness, according to the two scriptural sources.
In the defiled [dhyānas], there is no joy or bliss; there is clarity, discernment, mindfulness, and purity of equanimity and mindfulness; some also include pliancy and equanimity.
The fourth [dhyāna] is indeed immovable because it is free from the eight defects:
applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), the two breaths, and the four beginning with pleasure (sukha).
In the rebirths of the dhyānas, there are known to be mental joy and pleasure with equanimity, equanimity and mental joy,
pleasure and equanimity, and equanimity alone.

The body, eye, and ear consciousnesses, as well as that which originates informative action, belong to the first level when occurring in the second dhyāna and above; furthermore, they are undefiled-neutral.
One who does not possess it acquires the pure [attainment] through detachment or through rebirth;
however, one acquires the untainted through detachment, while the defiled is acquired through loss or through rebirth.
From the third [level] upwards and downwards, immediately after an untainted state, a wholesome state arises;
likewise, from a pure state, a defiled state of its own level also arises.
From a defiled [state], one enters its own pure or defiled [state], as well as the pure state of a lower level.
At the time of death, however, from a pure state one enters a defiled state; but from a defiled state, one does not enter a higher [level].
The pure [attainment] is fourfold, beginning with that conducive to decline, respectively;
for it is conducive to the arising of afflictions, to its own level, to a higher level, and to the outflow-free state.
Two, three, three, and one [respectively] follow immediately after the stages conducive to decline and so forth;
having gone and returned in two ways through the eight stages, they are practiced in close connection and by leaping over.
The leap-meditation attainment proceeds to the third level of a different category;
the dhyānas and formless attainments have their basis only in their own level or a lower level, for they do not depend on what is below.
However, at the peak of existence (bhavāgra), the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) occurs through the presence of the noble state of nothingness (ākiṃcanya).
Those [desire-realm thoughts] accompanied by craving take their own existence as an object; wholesome meditative absorption (dhyāna) has all things as its object.
The fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have lower contaminated states as their object;
defilements are abandoned by means of the uncontaminated [path] and by the preparatory stages.

The eight preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of these [dhyānas] are indeed characterized by neither-pain-nor-pleasure and are pure; the first is also noble (ārya), according to some, and is of three types; the intermediate dhyāna is without vitarka (atarka).
That [meditative attainment] is threefold and is neither-painful-nor-pleasant; it has the fruit of Great Brahma (mahābrahma).
The meditative absorption (samādhi) below that is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra; beyond that, it is without both.
The signless [concentration] proceeds by way of the aspects of the general characteristics; emptiness [proceeds] by way of the aspects of emptiness and non-self;
and the wishless [proceeds] by way of the other [remaining] aspects of the truths.
Those that are pure and stainless are the three doors to liberation;
these are the three other samādhis known as the emptiness of emptiness and so forth.
Two [samādhis] take the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) as their object, [the former] by way of emptiness and [the latter] by way of impermanence;
but the signless-within-the-signless takes it by way of peace, and the cessation-by-non-calculation takes destruction as its object.

The cultivation of concentration consisting of impure states among humans, excluding the seven preparatory stages, belongs to the immovable one; indeed, the first pure dhyāna is for the sake of happiness.
The supernormal knowledge of the eye is desired for seeing; those born of application are for the differentiation of wisdom;
that which is like a diamond, occurring in the final dhyāna, is the cultivation for the destruction of the outflows.
The four immeasurables are the antidotes to ill-will and the other [obstacles]:
loving-kindness is non-hatred; compassion is also [non-hatred]; sympathetic joy is gladness of mind.
The aspect [of this equanimity] is the desire for beings to be happy or, alas, to be free from suffering;
"may they rejoice"—this is directed toward sentient beings, and its object is indeed sentient beings of the desire realm.
Sympathetic joy (muditā) exists in two meditative absorptions (dhyāna); others [the remaining immeasurables] exist in six, though some say in five.
There is no abandonment through them; they are produced only among humans, and one who possesses them is certainly endowed with three.

There are eight liberations (vimokṣa). The first two are the meditation on the foul (aśubhā) and belong to the first two dhyānas. The third belongs to the last [dhyāna], and it is non-attachment (alobha). The pure formless [attainments] are meditative absorptions (samāhita).
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), however, follows immediately after the extremely subtle (sūkṣmasūkṣma).
Emergence from it occurs by means of a mind that is either pure of its own level or noble of a lower level.

The first [uncontaminated knowledges] have as their objects the visible things belonging to the desire realm; however, those that are formless have as their range the category of subsequent knowledge, the higher realms, and the suffering and so forth of their own level.
The eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana): the first two are like the first liberation;
the next two are like the second; the remaining four are like the pure liberation.
There are ten totalities (*kṛtsnāni*); eight are based on non-greed and belong to the final dhyāna.
Furthermore, their objects are the desire realm; two have the pure form and formless realms as their objects, while [the others] have their own four aggregates as their objects.
Cessation has been explained; however, the remainder is attained through the application of dispassion.
That which is designated as "formless" has its basis in the three realms, while the remainder is born of humans.
The production of the two formless realms occurs through the power of causes and karma;
however, in the realm of form, the production of the meditative absorptions occurs through those two as well as through the nature of things (dharmatā).
The True Dharma of the Teacher is twofold, consisting of scripture and realization;
its upholders are those who teach it and those who practice it.

This Abhidharma has been mostly explained by me according to the system established by the Vaibhāṣikas of Kaśmīra. Whatever has been poorly grasped herein is my own fault; regarding the principles of the True Dharma, the Sages are the authority.
When the Teacher, the eye of the world, had closed his eyes, and when the witnesses for the most part had passed away,
this teaching was thrown into disorder by base logicians who had not seen reality and were unrestrained.

Now that the Self-Existent One has attained supreme peace, and the upholders of the burden of the Self-Existent One’s teaching have also passed away, this world is without a protector; today it is being treated as it pleases by unrestrained views that destroy the spiritual community.
Thus, knowing that the Sage’s teaching has its life-breath at the throat and that it is the time of power for the defilements, those seeking liberation must not be negligent.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Abhidharmakośa, titled "Exposition of the Meditative Attainments."
